Calculating with rational numbers

If it gets 7 degrees colder at night, what does the thermometer show then? What is “minus times minus”? In this chapter you work out the rules for adding and subtracting on the number line, find the sign rules for multiplying from a pattern and calculate cleverly with the laws of arithmetic and the order of operations.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • add and subtract rational numbers, also with brackets and a minus sign in front
  • multiply and divide rational numbers and raise them to powers, with the sign rules
  • use the laws of arithmetic as shortcuts
  • apply the order of operations confidently

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Adding and subtracting

On the number line, adding a positive number means going to the right. Subtracting a positive number: going to the left. $-7 + 3$: start at −7, three to the right, finish at −4.

What about negative numbers? Getting a debt of €3 added is the same as giving away €3: $5 + (-3) = 5 - 3 = 2$. Having a debt of €3 taken away is as good as getting €3: $5 - (-3) = 5 + 3 = 8$.

In short: instead of subtracting a negative number, you add its opposite number. And adding a negative number means subtracting its absolute value.

KEY POINT · ADDING AND SUBTRACTING

$a + (-b) = a - b$   ·   $a - (-b) = a + b$

Same signs: add the absolute values, keep the sign: $-6 + (-5) = -11$

Different signs: subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger one, sign of the number with the larger absolute value: $-9 + 4 = -5$

Two minus signs in a row become a plus: $7 - (-2) = 7 + 2$.

Do not forget the brackets around negative numbers after an operation sign: $3 \cdot (-2)$, not $3 \cdot -2$.

INTERACTIVE · CALCULATING ON THE NUMBER LINE

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Multiplying, dividing and powers

$3 \cdot 3 = 9$, $3 \cdot 2 = 6$, $3 \cdot 1 = 3$, $3 \cdot 0 = 0$ – the result gets 3 smaller each time. If you continue this, you get $3 \cdot (-1) = -3$, $3 \cdot (-2) = -6$. And in the row $(-3) \cdot 2 = -6$, $(-3) \cdot 1 = -3$, $(-3) \cdot 0 = 0$ it gets 3 bigger each time: $(-3) \cdot (-1) = 3$.

When multiplying and dividing, you calculate with the absolute values and find the sign separately: two equal signs give plus, two different ones minus.

For powers of a negative number, it depends on the exponent: $(-2)^2 = 4$, $(-2)^3 = -8$. Careful: $-2^2$ means $-(2^2) = -4$.

KEY POINT · SIGN RULES

$(+) \cdot (+) = (+)$   ·   $(-) \cdot (-) = (+)$   ·   $(+) \cdot (-) = (-)$   ·   $(-) \cdot (+) = (-)$   – the same when dividing

Powers of a negative number: even exponent → positive, odd exponent → negative: $(-1)^4 = 1$, $(-1)^5 = -1$

Many factors: an even number of negative factors → positive, odd → negative

Memory aid: the enemy of my enemy is my friend – a mnemonic, not a reason. The pattern gives the reason.

Zero: you must not divide by 0, not with negative numbers either.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Laws of arithmetic and order of operations

$-37 + 58 + 37 - 8$: if you first combine $-37$ and $37$, you have 0 straight away and only need to work out $58 - 8 = 50$. The laws of arithmetic that you know from the natural numbers also hold for rational numbers.

When adding and multiplying you may swap and group differently. To do this, you write a subtraction as adding the opposite number: $58 - 8 = 58 + (-8)$. The distributive law helps with mental arithmetic: $7 \cdot (-98) = 7 \cdot (-100) + 7 \cdot 2$.

The order of operations stays the same: first brackets, then powers, then multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, otherwise from left to right.

KEY POINT · LAWS OF ARITHMETIC AND ORDER

Commutative law: $a + b = b + a$, $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$ · Associative law: $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$, $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$

Distributive law: $a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c$

Order: brackets → powers → multiplication and division → addition and subtraction

Do not swap: $5 - 3 \neq 3 - 5$ and $8 : 2 \neq 2 : 8$. Subtraction and division are not commutative.

Minus in front of a bracket: $-(3 - 8) = -3 + 8$; all the signs in the bracket turn round.

EXAMPLE 5 · A SHORTCUT

Calculate cleverly: $-25 + 17 + 25 - 7$

$(-25 + 25) + (17 - 7) = 0 + 10$

10

EXAMPLE 6 · ORDER OF OPERATIONS

Calculate: $3 - 2 \cdot (-4)^2$

Power: $(-4)^2 = 16$. Multiplication: $2 \cdot 16 = 32$. Subtraction: $3 - 32$.

−29

On five days these were measured in the morning: −4 °C, −1 °C, 2 °C, −5 °C, −2 °C. Calculate the mean.

Sum $-10$, mean $-10 : 5 = -2$ °C.

Fill in the number wall: each brick is the sum of the two below it. At the bottom are −3, 5, −8.

Middle: $-3 + 5 = 2$ and $5 + (-8) = -3$. Top: $2 + (-3) = -1$.

Three consecutive integers have the product −6. What are they?

The product is negative, so one or three of the numbers are negative. $(-3) \cdot (-2) \cdot (-1) = -6$. (With 1, 2, 3 it would be +6.)

EXCURSIONGIVING REASONS

Why minus times minus is plus

The pattern in unit 2 makes the rule believable. A real reason comes from the distributive law. We know: $1 + (-1) = 0$. So

$(-1) \cdot \big(1 + (-1)\big) = (-1) \cdot 0 = 0.$

If the distributive law is also to hold for negative numbers, the left-hand side is $(-1) \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot (-1) = -1 + (-1) \cdot (-1)$. That must give 0. So the only possibility is: $(-1) \cdot (-1) = 1$.

In 1867 the mathematician Hermann Hankel turned this into a principle: whoever extends a number range should keep the old laws of arithmetic. Then the new rules are not arbitrary – they are the only possible choice.

Source: Hermann Hankel, “Theorie der complexen Zahlensysteme”, Leipzig 1867 (principle of permanence).
